schools.summary: Ellicott names the design of the whole chapter — a magnificent contrast between human skill and Divine wisdom — and warns that the person spoken of throughout is man, not God.

Clarke calls it the oldest and finest piece of natural history in the world, fixing 'vein' (motsa) as a mine or 'going out'; Wesley sets the hymn in the flow of Job's argument about the depths of Divine wisdom.
Gill explains why silver is named before gold — first known and coined — and derives its name from a word for 'desire,' the vein running like veins in the body.
Henry states the governing lesson: the caverns of the earth may be discovered, but not the counsels of heaven.
Gill marks iron as the common, easily-won metal taken 'out of the dust,' and names Tubalcain, the heathen's Vulcan, instructor in brass and iron.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'he poureth forth stone as copper,' note that copper is the last-named metal binding the strophe, and weigh the observations of actual mining men.
Clarke argues nechushah is properly copper ('the stone is poured out for brass'), though the common rendering may point to the making of brass from copper and calamine.
Ellicott reads 'man setteth an end to darkness'; Keil and Delitzsch settle nachal as the perpendicular shaft and record the mining men's debate over 'valley' as a surface-vein.
Gill notes that some refer the verse to God but prefers the miner, whose lamp ends the darkness that reigned since the creation.
Clarke and Wesley take it of man's persevering industry into the shadow of death — 'stones of darkness' the gems hid where no living thing can dwell (Mr. Good, 'the region of darkness').

themes: the miner ends the ancient darkness
the stones of the shadow of death

schools.summary: Gill reads 'so that there is no inhabitant' — the miner flees when the usual flood of water breaks into the mine.
Clarke owns the verse 'very difficult,' adopting the mining sense (the drowned, abandoned shaft) while reporting Peters's navigation reading; Wesley keeps to the flooded mine drained by engines.
Ellicott calls it 'very uncertain,' offering either the shaft broken where none sojourns or the river whose course man so obliterates that men forget it was ever there.

debates.question: Does the obscure verse describe mining or navigation?

sides.position: mining — the inrushing flood that drowns and empties the shaft
navigation — a torrent or arm of the sea dividing nations until ships are found

schools.summary: Gill takes 'bread' for bread-corn, the wheat cast into the earth, with the traveller's lore of roots made into bread.

Keil and Delitzsch fix 'the earth' as the surface (adamah, a flat covering) set against 'that which is beneath'; Ellicott reads the miner's and the volcano's perpetual fires below the corn-bearing crust.
Clarke takes the 'fire' for a combustible fossil like coal, with an allusion to Sodom's overthrow; Wesley for coals and brimstone, unless a central fire be meant.

debates.question: What is the 'fire' turned up beneath the earth?

sides.position: combustible minerals dug by man — coal, brimstone
the earth's own subterranean or volcanic (central) fire

outliers.note: From the Vulgate's 'the land destroyed by fire' he draws a probable allusion to the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah, carried even into the pathless region of the next verses.

schools.summary: Gill takes the sapphire (sky-coloured, gold-flecked, a breastplate stone) for all precious stones, hearing in its blue the pavement under God's feet.

Keil and Delitzsch weigh whether the gold-dust belongs to the sapphire or names gold ore, and, with Schultens and Schlottmann, take it for gold ore; Ellicott lets the wonder of sapphire-stones and golden dust stand.
Clarke calls the place the gangue or matrix and reads plain gold dust; Wesley makes the dust a second kind of gold, distinct from that found in the mass.

themes: lapis lazuli and the true sapphire
the sapphire put for all gems

schools.summary: Gill makes the path the miners' track to the ores, unseen even by the eagle — quick-sighted king of birds — which is outdone by the labouring miner.

Clarke marvels at bird-instinct yet finds vulture's scent and eagle's eye useless here, and turns the verse against the confident geologists of his day; Wesley glosses the vulture's very quick and strong eye.

outliers.note: Records the Chaldee Targum's strange allegory — the path of the tree of life, unknown to Satan flying like a bird, unseen by the eye of Eve, unturned-to by the serpent.

themes: man alone finds the way down

schools.summary: Gill dwells on the ranging fierceness of the lion that searches every den yet never trod the miners' paths, and lifts it to the tyrant-persecutors who never trod the way of holiness ('children of pride').
Wesley notes that birds and beasts often lead men to hidden places, but never to these mines — the finding of them a special gift of God.
Henry sets the picture in its frame: the path untrodden by the lion's whelps that traverse all the paths of the wilderness.

themes: the mine a gift of God
the peak of the human triumph

schools.summary: Gill reads the miner setting his hammer to the rock, using fire and vinegar (Pliny) to split it and lay bare the ore within.
Ellicott reads tunnelling and canal-cutting so accurate the cisterns did not weep or trickle — the work of man over nature.
Clarke takes it of man overturning the mountains to extract the metals; Wesley alone refers this verse and the next two to God, whose works these are.

debates.question: Is the agent of the hand upon the rock (vv.9-11) man the miner or God?

sides.position: man the miner, in his excavating and tunnelling
God, whose eminent works overturn the rocks and produce new rivers

schools.summary: Gill reads the miner cleaving rocks and opening courses to drain his workings, sometimes sunk forty or fifty fathom deep till the water defeats him.
Keil and Delitzsch work at 'rivers among the rocks,' rejecting the 'gathering of drippings' reading and finding a sense of restraining or binding the water (cf. the Arabic for a dam).
Clarke describes canals, adits, and levels driven far underground; Wesley notes the eye that sees precious things no human art was able to discover.

themes: the eye that sees every precious thing

schools.summary: Gill renders 'he bindeth the floods from weeping' — the miner stops every passage so close the water cannot ooze or drop like a tear.
Clarke reads the miner turning rivers from their beds to reach what lay hidden, crowning the note with Pliny's descent into the bowels of the earth and Ovid's lament over the iron age.
Henry closes the mining hymn: the hidden brought to light and refined — 'Go to the miners, thou sluggard in religion, and be wise'; better to get wisdom than gold.

themes: the close of the mining hymn

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch mark that the question is the designed end of the mining description, the article giving wisdom its transcendency, and distinguish 'understanding' (right criteria) from 'wisdom' (things in their final causes); Ellicott feels the sublime effect of the timing.
Gill draws the contrast of the 'but' — every precious thing is wrung from the earth, but wisdom has no vein and no place to be found.
Henry names the jewel now sought, the knowing of God and ourselves, greater than all natural philosophy; two things cannot be found — its price and its place.
Clarke insists the terms mean true religion, another word for happiness, come only by revelation; Wesley grants man the wisdom of nature and art but not the sublime wisdom of the knowledge of God.
Gill takes the price of the worth men fail to set and the equivalent none can find, or 'the order thereof,' the disposal of Providence; the Gospel and Christ himself despised by carnal men.
Keil and Delitzsch read 'the land of the living' as the whole world a man might search — the deep, the sea — without laying hold of wisdom as of a buried ore.
Clarke: wisdom is of infinite value, the only science of both worlds; without it the wisest man is a beast, and the world by its own wisdom never knew God.
Henry finds two faults — few value wisdom (the cock and the barley-corn), and none can buy it, for it is the Holy Ghost's gift, without money and without price (Acts 8:20).
Gill makes the depth the dug mines, which could they speak would own they hold no ore of the value of wisdom.
Keil and Delitzsch read the abyss and the sea as declaring that wisdom lies in no bounded space and is had by no direct exchange.
Clarke turns the personification into a parable that every voyage and enjoyment proclaims 'true happiness is not here'; Wesley: not found in any part of the sea, nor learned from any creature.
Henry: ask the miners (the depth) and the mariners (the sea) — men break greater difficulties for the world's wealth than the next world's wisdom.

themes: the depth and the sea disclaim it

schools.summary: Gill fastens on the word for gold that signifies 'shut up' — shut in the earth, then among men's treasures — so 'gold shall not be given instead of it.'
Clarke urges the example of Solomon, who had all gold could buy and wisdom besides, yet not this wisdom, so all was vanity.
Henry: not all the substance of a man's house could be a valuable consideration for wisdom, the Holy Ghost's gift, come without money and without price.
Keil and Delitzsch render that pure gold cannot be given nor silver weighed as its price, leading into the catalogue of gems that follows.

outliers.note: Takes the verse to fit a Solomonic authorship of the book — the sentiments such as we might expect from the wisest yet unsatisfied of men.

schools.summary: Gill names the gold of Ophir and the breastplate stones onyx and sapphire, none of the value of wisdom; 'valued' may be read 'strowed,' as goods set to sale.
Clarke lays out the whole treasury of golds and gems and corrects the sapphire — not our modern stone but the lapis lazuli, blue with golden pyrites, whence ultramarine is ground.
Keil and Delitzsch render that wisdom is not outweighed with Ophir's gold nor the precious onyx and sapphire, one couplet among many that abase every jewel.

outliers.note: Argues the biblical 'sapphire' is really lapis lazuli, not the modern sapphire, and that the old gem-names are throughout uncertain.

themes: the ancient sapphire as lapis lazuli

schools.summary: Gill canvasses crystal (once far more prized, Pliny's costly vessel, Nero's broken cups), amber, and glass (from Phoenicia, the Belus, Sidon) — none able to equal wisdom.

Keil and Delitzsch settle on glass for the transparent thing named; Ellicott reads 'the attraction of it,' finds comment superfluous before the passage's sublimity, and notes the likeness to Proverbs 8.

debates.question: Does the transparent treasure (zekukith) name crystal, glass, or amber?

schools.summary: Gill names coral (Coralia on the Red Sea) and pearls, but owns the Hebrew words uncertain — left untranslated by some, taken by others for stones found in high places.
Keil and Delitzsch render that pearls and crystal are not to be mentioned and the getting of wisdom is beyond corals, among the costly chapatzim.
Clarke identifies coral (grows head downwards) and pearls (formed coat on coat), and raises whether peninim means rubies or the loadstone, whose 'attraction' wisdom exceeds.

debates.question: Does peninim mean rubies or the loadstone (magnet)?

sides.position: rubies, the blood-red stone (the common rendering)
the loadstone, whose attraction wisdom surpasses
holders: some learned men (as reported by Clarke)

schools.summary: Gill places the topaz not in Abyssinia but in the Arabian Cush near Midian and Job's country (whence Zipporah), citing Diodorus and Strabo on the isle of serpents.
Clarke reads Cush as the Ethiopia from the Red Sea coast toward Lower Egypt, repeating Diodorus's account but doubting its correctness as too much a legend.
Keil and Delitzsch render that the topaz of Ethiopia is not equal to wisdom, nor she outweighed by pure fine gold — the verdict that closes the inventory.

debates.question: What is the 'Ethiopia' (Cush) whose topaz is named?

sides.position: the Arabian Cush near Midian and Job's own country
the African Ethiopia from the Red Sea coast toward Lower Egypt

outliers.note: Doubts the correctness of Diodorus's tale of the topaz-bearing isle of serpents, judging it too much in the form of a legend.

schools.summary: Gill: the same questions are repeated to set forth wisdom's excellency and carry the discourse forward.
Henry dwells on the repeated question: God's secret will is out of reach, the plummet of reason cannot fathom the abyss of the divine counsels — God now a God that hideth himself (Isa. 45:15).
Clarke notes the words nearly the same as before; Wesley finds by the inquiry a twofold wisdom — one hid in God, the other revealed to man.
Gregory the Great reads the veiling as a lesson in self-abasement — if the invisible created things escape our eyes, no wonder the Eternal Wisdom does — God reserving his Appearance for the Elect.
Gill takes 'all living' of rational men, not the beasts; the wisdom of God, his spiritual wisdom, the Gospel, and Christ himself hidden from the most prudent natural men.
Wesley: the plummet of reason cannot sound the abyss of the divine counsels; be content not to know Providence's events till time, nor its reasons till eternity.
Henry: hid from philosophers, politicians, and saints, and kept close from the high-flying fowls that behold afar off (ch. 39:29) — man wiser than they, yet coming short.

outliers.note: Allegorizes the 'fowls of the air' as sometimes the powers of the air, the evil spirits that, like the birds devouring the wayside seed, pluck the word of life from men's memory.

schools.summary: Gill takes destruction and death for the region of the dead, whose records yield of wisdom but a distant fame.

Keil and Delitzsch render 'with our ears we heard a report of it,' the realm of Abaddon below able to give but an echo; Ellicott finds it natural that death should hear wisdom's fame, since wisdom departs from the evil leading to their abode.
Clarke identifies Abaddon/Apollyon with the great enemy (Rev. 9:11); Wesley hears a gleam beyond the grave — Death saying, 'I will fetch thee shortly where even this wisdom shall be found.'

outliers.note: Reads 'Abaddon and death' as the destroyer Apollyon and his offspring, who have only heard wisdom's fame because it is point-blank contrary to the empire of death (Rev. 9:11).

schools.summary: Gill: God and God only understands the way wisdom itself takes and the grounds of its course; applied to Christ, the wisdom of God, whose way in the covenant God alone comprehends.

Clarke draws that wisdom can be taught only by God's own revelation, noting a variant ('hath established' for 'understandeth,' 6 MSS and the LXX); Wesley: God alone knows the methods and the place, which is only in his own mind.
Ellicott reflects that wisdom's relation to man implies the existence of evil (wrong is what is wrung aside from the right), and turns toward the Gospel — wisdom purchasable by the poor (Isa. 55:1).

outliers.note: Notes a textual variant — six MSS and the Septuagint read 'God hath well established her way' for 'God understandeth the way thereof.'
Meditates that the existence of wisdom for man implies the existence of evil, and that Job's wisdom, though not the Gospel, is illustrated by Isaiah's free grace and Christ's pearl of great price.

schools.summary: Gill reads the verse as the ground of God's sole knowledge — all quarters of the earth and all things in them lie open to him, so no way or place of wisdom can escape him.
Clarke: his knowledge unlimited and his power infinite; Wesley: his providence infinite and universal, reaching all places and times, where men have but narrow understandings.
Henry: God omniscient, looking to the ends of the earth in place and time, his eyes running to and fro, so that he alone is a competent judge of every part and every man's affairs.

themes: omniscience the ground of knowing wisdom
the miner's lamp and the divine gaze

schools.summary: Gill: God makes the wind, holds it in his fists, gives it its bent and force, and can add to or take from its weight so it presses more or less.

Clarke reads the 'weight for the winds' as the atmosphere's gravity, nicely proportioned for life, and the waters weighed as the sea's due proportion to the land; Wesley: God manages the winds by weight, instancing the lightest things to prove his exactness in all.

Henry marvels that what is lighter than the wind is yet poised (Ps. 135:7), the tides and showers weighed and measured — and if Providence be so exact here, how much more in dispensing frowns and favours.

themes: reading his justice off his precision

schools.summary: Gill: God decreed within himself to give the rain, his gift alone; the thunder his voice (plural, its many claps), the lightning going with it, seen before heard.
Keil and Delitzsch render the decree for rain and the course for the lightning, carrying it into the seeing and declaring of wisdom that follows.

Clarke traces the physics of rain (vapour, cloud, condensation) and reads the word for lightning from a root meaning to notch — the zigzag of the flash; Wesley refers the decree to the fixed statute-law set at creation.
Gill takes the 'it' for God's own wisdom, seen in himself and in his works, approved as very good and declared to men by nature and providence.

Ellicott parses the four verbs — seeing (intuition), declaring (ratiocination), preparing (determination), searching out (investigation) — each implying mind, against the fatality of blind law; Keil and Delitzsch render the taking of wisdom as a pattern and its testing.

Clarke: when God had tried and proved his finished work he gave the needful revelation; Wesley guards 'searched out' as no ignorance in God but the perfection of his wisdom, spoken after the manner of men.
Henry notes some read wisdom here as a person, 'then he saw her and showed her,' anticipating the essential Wisdom of the Father, the eternal Word (Prov. 8:22; John 1).

outliers.note: Records the reading of Wisdom as a person — 'then he saw her and showed her' — pointing to the eternal Word who was by God before ever the earth was (Prov. 8:22; John 1:1).

themes: God saw, declared, prepared, searched out wisdom

schools.summary: Gill weighs whether the word is spoken 'unto Adam' or, as he prefers, in general to the sons of men — the whole of man being to fear God and keep his commandments.

Clarke reads the revelation given Adam after his fall (who sought wisdom in a forbidden way, Gen. 3:6), the cure being to fear the Lord and depart from evil; Wesley: spoken to Adam and in him to all his posterity, and Job's own self-vindication against the charge of hypocrisy.
Ellicott holds it no bare history but universally true — man's primary revelation — and notes the divine name here is Adonai, not the Jehovah Job used in ch. 12:9.
Henry: the fear of the Lord the spring and summary of all religion, a filial fear showing itself in departing from evil — agreeing exactly with God's character of Job (ch. 1:1).

debates.question: To whom is 'unto man he said' addressed — Adam, or mankind in general?

sides.position: to Adam the first man (and in him his posterity)
to the sons of men in general

outliers.note: Marks that 'the Lord' here is Adonai, not the four-lettered Jehovah used by Job earlier (ch. 12:9), the name later everywhere substituted by the Jews.

themes: the fear of the Lord is wisdom
the address to Adam or mankind
the close of the hymn and Job's self-vindication
